subject: Size allometry in total shape but not PC1

messages.author: 62a7fe14c0ce6d79
messages.subject: Size allometry in total shape but not PC1
parts:
Hello geomorph group
I'm getting some results that are hard to explain. I have a dataset of 59 landmarks on 29 specimens (hippopotamus crania). When I look at the relationship of log centroid size to total shape (using coords from the gm.prcomp object), there is strong size-allometry, as expected. However when I plot PC1 against log centroid size, there is no relationship (see both plots attached - note the y axis on the second plot is not a regression score but the actual PC1 values). 

In my experience, size allometry is usually expressed along PC1 (which in this data explains 45% of the variation), and plots of coords~size or PC1~size should be very similar. 

Are there cases of size-allometry being highly significant in total shape but not in any of the major PCs? I've checked my data several times and I can't seem to find any obvious errors in the landmarks or in the analysis script. When I separately test each of the 29 PCs against log Csize (proc.lm), the only PC with a significant relationship with size is, bizarrely, PC15 (p<0.001, R2=0.26). Has anything like this been documented before? Or where might the problem lie?

Thanks for any input.

Faysal Bibi
Museum für Naturkunde, Berlin

messages.author: f16866fc42d43e64
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Size allometry in total shape but not PC1
parts:
Faysal,

contrary to your intuition (which I understand might come from other analyses you have previously conducted), I would not necessarily expect PC1 to align with allometric shape variation. This depends a lot on the system you are working with and the composition of your sample. If you are working with males and females of a strongly dimorphic species (in shape, that is), allometry may only appear as a minor source of variation. Or if you are working with a macroevolutionary sample of many species of similar size, again, size-related variation may be minor. Remember that PC1 knows nothing about size, sex, species, or any other source of variation.

Given this, and being naive about your system and sample, I do not see anything strange in this result, neither do I think it is worth searching for errors. Allometry is just not a major source of variation in this sample, at least not to be captured by PC1. This does not mean that there is no significant allometry (which your results are telling you there is).

I hope this helps,
Antigoni

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Size allometry in total shape but not PC1
parts:
Dear Antigoni

Thank you for your quick reply. Indeed these are highly dimorphic species, and the sample includes males and females and a range of ages from infants to old adults. Presumably the ontogenetic signal and sexual dimorphism would combine to produce diverging allometric trends in males and females as they increase in size, and that this would show up as PC1. But the sex information we have (which is incomplete) suggests this is not the case. Perhaps the little sex info we have on the museum labels is incorrect.

We'll keep digging and exploring the shape changes associated with PC1. It’s reassuring to know there is not necessarily a problem with the data or the analysis.

Best
Faysal
